46.0.s.en: 1. God, the bearer of our burdens:

46.0.0.en: 1 “Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth, their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast. 2 They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity. 3 Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb: 4 And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you. 5 To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like? 6 They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, and hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship. 7 They bear him upon the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place, and he standeth; from his place shall he not remove: yea, one shall cry unto him, yet can he not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.”

46.0.1.en: God compares the gods of Babylon with Himself: the former need someone to carry them, but He is the bearer of our lives with all their troubles, for He says:

46.0.2.en: “Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth, their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast. They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity” [1-2].

46.0.3.en: The two chief gods of Babylon were shaken before Cyrus and bowed down to him, so the two objects of worship became slaves, carried with all their statues on animals without power, since all were unable to walk, indeed unable even to move. All the jewels that adorn the statues were taken by... and Cyrus came and all were taken into captivity... Can these two objects of worship deliver anyone, as long as they are unable even to save themselves?!

46.0.4.en: “Bel”: an Akkadian name corresponding to the Hebrew name “Baal,” meaning “lord”; perhaps he is the very god Marduk (Jer 50:2; 51:44); he is the god of the sun and the god of spring. He has the form of a great man with a crown on his head and seven bull horns. Food and drink were offered to him in large quantities every evening, and they believed that he ate and drank them, until the prophet Daniel disclosed to the king the existence of a secret door in the temple through which the priests entered with their families at night to eat the food and drink in secret, as is recorded in the story of Bel in the additions to Daniel.

46.0.5.en: “Nebo”: a Babylonian name meaning “announcer,” the god of science and knowledge; Borsippa, near Babylon, was the center of his worship. The kings of Babylon sought blessing by him and bore his name together with their original names, such as Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan and Nebushasban.

46.1.0.en: These two gods were exposed, and their inability to move or to protect their adornment was disgraced before Cyrus. But the living God is the Savior of His people; He bears our burdens when we have not yet been formed in our mothers’ wombs, until we reach old age, for He affirms to us, “I am he... I will bear” [4]. It is as though He says: I have myriads of angels and the heavenly creation and many prophets, priests and servants... but I place Myself in the hands of My people to bear their troubles Myself, and to take their sins away from them, and to support them in all their responsibilities... I bear them Myself as upon My shoulders.

46.1.1.en: This is what God affirms throughout the generations, saying: “Behold, I will inquire after my sheep and visit them... I will feed my flock, and I will cause them to lie down, saith the Lord GOD. I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but I will destroy the fat and the strong; I will feed them with judgment... Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle” (Ezek 34:11-22). Thus He affirms: “I am he... I will bear.”

46.1.2.en: God our Savior does not cease to call us to Himself that He may bear our burdens, saying: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mt 11:28). Therefore it is said of Him: “Surely he hath borne our griefs” (Isa 53:4); “he bare the sin of many” (Isa 53:12); “the God of our salvation bears us” (Ps 68:19).

46.1.3.en: Our Lord Jesus came as a Savior not only to bear our burdens and our sins, atoning for them, but to bear us in Himself; He captivates us by His love to lift us up with Him to His glory. He came down to us to bear us in Himself, that we may ascend in Him and by Him to His Kingdom.

46.1.4.en: We return to His address in the Book of Isaiah: “I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you” [4].

46.1.5.en: “I have made,” that is, I allowed the Babylonian captivity in order to expose your weaknesses.

46.1.6.en: “And I will bear” (I lift up): I remove this shame from you and arrange your release from captivity.

46.1.7.en: “And I will carry”: I Myself take up the bearing of your troubles... I am the hidden God.

46.1.8.en: “And I will deliver you”: I bring you into freedom, and return you to the land of promise, and save you.

46.1.9.en: This is the work of God the Savior: He makes, He lifts up, He bears, and He saves. He allows our sins to be exposed so that we may realize that we are captives, not in the captivity of Babylon, but under the captivity of the devil and his evil works; and He lifts up as He removes this shame from us by His divine plan for our salvation; and He bears as He took away the debt Himself on our behalf and did not entrust our salvation to an angel or an archangel or a prophet; and finally He saves when He carries us to His heavens and grants us fellowship in His divine glories.

46.1.10.en: The Apostle Paul says: “Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28). The Lord Christ bowed His back to bear the sins of the whole world, for He died for all, but He is counted a Savior for the believers alone, those who accepted that the weight of their sins be lifted from them, so that they are borne as righteous in Him and He enters with them into the bosom of His Father.

46.1.11.en: * He died for all, that is on His part, for this death was the counterpart against the perishing of all humanity, but He did not bear the sins of all people because they did not wish it.

46.1.12.en: * The lamb of Moses (the Passover) did not bear at once the sins of anyone, but this Lamb bore the sins of the whole world, for since the world was in danger of perishing, He hastened and saved it from the wrath of God.

46.1.13.en: * They heard that He bears the sins of the world (Jn 1:36), and at once they ran to Him, saying: If it is possible for Him to remove the accusations directed against us, why do we delay? Here is the One who saves without toil on our part.

46.1.14.en: St. John Chrysostom * By the Cross He gave salvation to the world.

46.1.15.en: No human being in history attained the greatness that qualifies him to take away the sin of the whole world, neither Enoch nor Abraham nor Isaac, even though he offered himself to death, but he was spared, since he was not able to remove the stain of sin.

46.1.16.en: Who, then, is this great Man by whose death sin dies?! This cannot be one of human beings... But God chose the Son, the Son of God who is over all, and He is the One who can be offered for the sins of all!

46.1.17.en: It was necessary for Him to die, because by His victory over death He is able to rescue the others who are like slain men lying in the graves.

46.1.18.en: He broke the bondage of the passions, and the chains of death were not able to hold Him!

46.1.19.en: St. Ambrose * Loose my pains by Your pains; heal my wounds by Your wounds; cleanse my blood with Your blood, and mingle in my body the fragrance of life that belongs to Your holy Body!

46.1.20.en: The Spiritual Elder The Lord bore our sins with all their weight in His body in order to grant us His righteousness in us, and we ourselves became borne in Him by His Holy Spirit so that He might lift us up to His heavens. He is the One who earlier bore His old people out of the land of bondage with all its weight and bitterness, to bring them into the land of promise, indeed to bring them to Himself. “I bare you on eagles’ wings, and brought you unto myself” (Ex 19:4); “thou hast seen how that the LORD thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went, until ye came into this place” (Deut 1:31).

46.1.21.en: God has affirmed His surpassing love for us: He bears us while we are in the womb and remains bearing us until old age [3-4]. This surpasses the love of a mother who is able to carry her child in the womb, or the infant, and to some extent when he becomes a little child in the first few years of his life... She carries him bodily and bears some of his troubles, but she is unable to grasp all his hidden secrets in order to share his troubles. But God bears us until old age; He bears all our troubles, visible and hidden, and as the psalmist says: “My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord embraces me” (Ps 27:10).

46.2.0.en: In His love God has no like, neither the parents nor the other gods who need someone to make them, and lift them on the shoulder, and set them in a place, and guard them lest they be stolen; their worshipers cry out to them, but they do not answer them in the time of distress [5-7].

46.3.s.en: 2. The calling of Cyrus from the east:

46.3.0.en: 8 “Remember this, and shew yourselves men: bring it again to mind, O ye transgressors. 9 Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me, 10 Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure: 11 Calling a ravenous bird from the east, the man that executeth my counsel from a far country: yea, I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed it, I will also do it. 12 Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness: 13 I bring near my righteousness; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not tarry: and I will place salvation in Zion for Israel my glory.”

46.4.0.en: This is the pleasure of God [10]: that He worked in the past and still works and remains working for the salvation of His people. He bore their burdens in the days of Moses when they came out of Egypt, and He bears them during their return from the Babylonian captivity, and He still bears them through the standing sacrifice of the Cross.

46.5.0.en: Cyrus, a symbol of the Lord Christ, was called the ravenous bird [11] because he is swift in movement and strong, swooping down on Babylon to seize it like prey, seizing its gods and its treasures... He is a symbol of the Lord Christ, who swooped down on the enemy of good and shattered his kingdom to restore to man his dignity, his freedom and his spiritual wealth.

46.5.1.en: “The man that executeth my counsel from a far country” [11], a symbol of the Lord Christ who came from heaven to become the “Son of Man” (the man of My counsel), who fulfills the will of the Father in Himself with pleasure.

46.6.0.en: The prophet Isaiah sees the Savior coming from afar, so he calls the distant Gentiles to draw near to Him and enjoy His righteousness and salvation: “Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness: I bring near my righteousness; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not tarry” [12-13].

46.6.1.en: Perhaps here he directs his address to the hard-hearted Babylonians, announcing to them that their resistance to God’s righteousness and salvation will not last, for the time of salvation has drawn near.

46.6.2.en: And perhaps he is speaking to the hard-hearted Gentiles so that they may accept the righteousness of the Lord and His salvation without resistance.

47.0.0.en: 1 “Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate. 2 Take the millstones, and grind meal: uncover thy locks, make bare the leg, uncover the thigh, pass over the rivers. 3 Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and I will not meet thee as a man. 4 As for our redeemer, the LORD of hosts is his name, the Holy One of Israel. 5 Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms.”

47.0.1.en: “Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate” [1].

47.0.2.en: Babylon was called “the virgin”; this comparison is used in the Holy Bible concerning cities (Isa 1:8; 37:22; Jer 31:21; 46:11; Lam 1:15). This virgin is either betrothed to God as a holy bride to Him, like Jerusalem, or betrothed to the enemy of good and becomes his bride, united to him, bearing his kingdom of darkness.

47.0.3.en: Since Babylon represents the soul that has fallen through pride, together with luxury and temporal joy and the seeking of earthly passions, what befell her reveals what happens to man because of sin.

47.0.4.en: What befell Babylon? Or what are the fruits of sin?

47.0.5.en: a. Being the capital of the greatest state of that time, she inclined to care for the show of splendor while practicing corruption; she had the appearance of outward joy, so intense grief befell her and she came down to the dust [1], as though she had lost her husband or one of her loved ones (Josh 7:6; Job 2:12; 10:9; Ps 22:15; Lam 3:29).

47.0.6.en: The first work of sin is the loss of inner joy and the peace that passes understanding, so the soul is filled with bitterness and despair, with a feeling of isolation and deprivation.

47.0.7.en: * Yes, my God... in the absence of Your light there is an appearance of death, or rather a coming of nothingness....

47.0.8.en: Woe is me... many wounds have befallen me, and although You are the Comforter, the Giver of peace, I have gone far from You.

47.0.9.en: Woe is me... many follies have overtaken me, and although You are the Truth, I did not seek counsel from You...

47.0.10.en: My evils caused me deep wounds, for I did not walk in the narrow way; although You are the Life, I was not with You.

47.0.11.en: St. Augustine b. Instead of the throne, the “chair,” and authority, Babylon sits on the ground in humiliation as a captive [1]

47.0.12.en: God created man as lord over the earth and granted him dignity and authority, but pride brought him down to the abyss. Man became in the humiliation of slaves, bowing to sin and led after the lusts of the flesh like a slave, after he had been a king who knew how to direct his feelings and his senses and all his energies for the sake of the Kingdom of God. Therefore it is said: “he that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city” (Prov 16:32).

47.0.13.en: The Holy Bible warns us of pride: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud” (Prov 16:18-19).

47.0.14.en: * Temporal glory is like a hidden rock in the sea, unknown to the sailor until a ship strikes it and its bottom is torn and fills with water.

47.1.0.en: St. Isaac the Syrian c. After Babylon had been the lady of the haughty kingdoms, she became one who performs the hard works of slaves for the sake of her masters. Here the prophet Isaiah depicts her as a woman grinding with the millstone, a work that needs two women working together; and the great millstone is turned by animals; yet here she is commanded to do this violent work without help from anyone [2]. She becomes like Samson when sin humbled him and he began to turn the mill in place of the animals, so that all laughed at him and mocked him.

47.1.1.en: When St. John Chrysostom speaks of our ascent to the heavens in Christ Jesus who ascended, he reveals to us how our life and nature descended until we became lower than the animals, but our Christ lifted us out of this humiliation by His ascension and granted us the enjoyment of His heavens, for he says: [Look at our nature, how it was lowered and then raised. For it was not possible to descend further than man descended, nor possible to ascend higher than Christ was raised... Paul makes this clear when he says: “He that descended is the same also that ascended.” Where did He descend? “Into the lower parts of the earth”; and He ascended “far above all heavens” (Eph 4:9-10)... We were nothing but dust and ashes... We became more foolish than the irrational animals, for man came to be compared with them and became like them (Ps 49:20; Isa 1:3)... See how we became more foolish than the ass and the ox (Isa 1:3), and than the birds of the heaven, the turtle and the swallow (Jer 8:7)... We became disciples of the ants (Prov 6:6)... more rigid than stones (Isa 6:2), we are likened to serpents (Ps 58:5)... we are called children of the devil (Jn 8:44)... Such became our lowliness and unworthiness... But today our nature has been raised above every creature. Today the angels have recovered those whom they lost long ago! Today the archangels have seen those whom they have long desired to see! Today they have seen our nature on the divine throne, shining in eternal beauty and everlasting glory!].

47.1.2.en: e. “Uncover thy locks, make bare the leg” [2]; this is a thing unbecoming for young noble girls at that time, to uncover their faces or to gather up the hem of their garments.

47.2.0.en: After she had been sailing with her commercial or war ships, adorned and of great price, as the queen of the world, it is said to her: “make bare the leg, pass over the rivers. Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and I will not meet thee as a man” [3]. She shattered many and wronged many nations, so she deserved that her work should return upon her and she should bear the same shame. It is as though sin brings man into shame and disgrace.

47.2.1.en: Sin caused us to lose the garments of divine grace, so we became naked; but our Christ, who bears our sins, was stripped for our sake, to offer Himself as a garment covering our shame.

47.2.2.en: * Those who crucified Him stripped Him of His garments like butchers, but He was silent like a sheep before the butcher!

47.2.3.en: He left His garment when He rejoiced (at the wedding of the Cross), that those who went out of Paradise naked might put it on!

47.2.4.en: He clothes them with His garments and remains Himself in mockery, because He knew that they were fitting for exposed Adam!

47.2.5.en: They stripped off His garments and put on Him a scarlet robe, the color of blood, so that the slain (sacrificed) Bridegroom might be adorned with it!

47.3.0.en: St. Jacob of Serug f. She enters a state of bewilderment and gloom because of the disaster that befalls her, and becomes unable to speak, living in darkness: “Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms” [5].

47.4.0.en: 6 “I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst shew them no mercy; upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke. 7 And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: so that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it. 8 Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children: 9 But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood: they shall come upon thee in their perfection for the multitude of thy sorceries, and for the great abundance of thine enchantments. 10 For thou hast trusted in thy wickedness: thou hast said, None seeth me. Thy wisdom and thy knowledge, it hath perverted thee; and thou hast said in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me. 11 Therefore shall evil come upon thee; thou shalt not know from whence it riseth: and mischief shall fall upon thee; thou shalt not be able to put it off: and desolation shall come upon thee suddenly, which thou shalt not know. 12 Stand now with thine enchantments, and with the multitude of thy sorceries, wherein thou hast laboured from thy youth; if so be thou shalt be able to profit, if so be thou mayest prevail. 13 Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee. 14 Behold, they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them; they shall not deliver themselves from the power of the flame: there shall not be a coal to warm at, nor fire to sit before it. 15 Thus shall they be unto thee with whom thou hast laboured, even thy merchants, from thy youth: they shall wander every one to his quarter; none shall save thee.”

47.4.1.en: The decree for the collapse of Babylon was issued, but not without grounds for this judgment, for God in His love always declares to those who fall under judgment the reasons for the verdict, so that others may take warning and not fall into the same sins. As for the sins of Babylon, they are:

47.4.2.en: a. Violence and lack of mercy. God allowed His people to be handed over to Babylon for discipline, but Babylon exploited the situation and practiced violence even on the elders, with no regard for their helplessness because of their old age [6]. God was expecting from her gentleness toward His people, whom He loves even in the moments of handing them over to discipline.

47.5.0.en: b. She thought she was above the law; in her use of violence she did not realize that what she does to others will come upon her, and with the measure she measures it will be measured to her. She thought she was lady of all and did not remember her latter end [7].

47.6.0.en: c. Her clinging to deceptive security or false peace [8], which is not based on the soul’s meeting with God, the source of peace, but on man’s belief that nothing will befall him because of his vain greatness or his position or his wealth. She reckoned that she would not become a widow nor bereaved of children, relying on sorcery and enchantments, so she was deceived, and widowhood and bereavement came upon her suddenly in one day [9]. She became a widow because she lost the kingship, and she became bereaved by the slaughter of her inhabitants, who were as sons and daughters to her.

47.7.0.en: d. Her ignoring that God sees her and knows her secrets: “For thou hast trusted in thy wickedness: thou hast said, None seeth me” [10].

47.7.1.en: e. Her reliance on mere human wisdom [10], together with resorting to sorcery and enchantments, for she reckoned that the stargazers could save her in the time of distress by their counsel and their knowledge of the unseen, but they themselves burn like stubble and do not escape from the flame [11-15]. There was no state in the world known for sorcerers and astrologers like her (see the Book of Daniel), and here the prophet mocks them.
